case: Madhub Chunder Poramanick v Rajcoomar Doss
lawyer_note: Partial restraints are void too; no reasonableness test outside the statutory exception.

case: Brahmaputra Tea Co Ltd v Scarth
lawyer_note: Covenant operating during service upheld; the part operating after it ended held void.
holding: Under s.27 a covenant stopping an employee from taking service with others after the agreed term is void, but a promise to serve one employer exclusively during the term is lawful, so the clause fails only so far as it operates after the term.

case: Niranjan Shankar Golikari v Century Spinning and Manufacturing Co Ltd
lawyer_note: A negative covenant operating during the term of the contract is not a restraint of trade.
holding: A negative covenant that stops an employee from working for others only during the term of the employment contract is not a restraint of trade under s.27, unless the contract is unconscionable, excessively harsh, unreasonable or one-sided.

case: Superintendence Company of India (P) Ltd v Krishan Murgai
lawyer_note: Restraint operating after the contract ends is void under s.27.
holding: A clause restraining an employee who 'leaves' service covers only a voluntary departure, not a dismissal by the employer; the majority left s.27 undecided, while A.P. Sen J held that a service covenant operating after the employment ends is void under s.27.

case: Gujarat Bottling Co Ltd v Coca Cola Co
lawyer_note: Negative stipulation during a franchise term not void, unless unconscionable, excessively harsh or one-sided.
holding: A negative stipulation in a commercial agreement that bars dealing in competing products only while the agreement subsists is not a restraint of trade void under s.27, unless the contract is wholly one-sided.

case: Percept D'Mark (India) (P) Ltd v Zaheer Khan
lawyer_note: Restrictive covenant extending beyond the term is void; reasonableness is not the test under s.27.
holding: Under s.27 a restrictive covenant that extends beyond the term of the contract is void whether or not it is reasonable or partial, unless it falls within the statutory exception.

lawyer_note: Parties may choose one of several competent courts; this does not offend s.28.
holding: Parties cannot by agreement give jurisdiction to a court that has none under the Code of Civil Procedure, but where two or more courts have jurisdiction an agreement to sue in only one of them is not against public policy and does not contravene s.28.

case: A.B.C. Laminart (P) Ltd v A.P. Agencies
lawyer_note: Same, and parties cannot confer jurisdiction on a court that has none.
holding: A clear and unambiguous agreement to sue in one of several courts that already have jurisdiction is not hit by ss.23 or 28, but the other competent courts are excluded only if the clause excludes them clearly, so 'subject to Kaira jurisdiction' did not bar a suit at Salem.

case: Swastik Gases (P) Ltd v Indian Oil Corporation Ltd
lawyer_note: Exclusive jurisdiction clause read as excluding other competent courts even without words like 'only'.
holding: Where two or more courts have jurisdiction, a clause making the agreement 'subject to the jurisdiction of the courts at Kolkata' impliedly excludes all other courts even without words like 'only', 'alone' or 'exclusive', and such a clause does not offend s.28.

case: Food Corporation of India v New India Assurance Co Ltd
limb: s.28(a), second limb, and s.28(b) (time limits)
lawyer_note: Pre-amendment distinction between limiting time to sue and extinguishing the right.
holding: A clause requiring a claim to be lodged with the insurer within six months does not shorten the time to sue, so a suit filed within the ordinary limitation period after a timely claim is maintainable, Sahai J adding that such a clause is a condition precedent and not a limit void under the pre-1997 s.28.

case: National Insurance Co Ltd v Sujir Ganesh Nayak & Co
limb: s.28(a), second limb, and s.28(b) (time limits)
lawyer_note: Same distinction, applied to an insurance policy.
holding: Under s.28 as it stood before 1997, a clause shortening the limitation period for a suit is void, but a clause that extinguishes the right itself if not exercised within a set period is valid, so an insurance condition ending the insurer's liability 12 months after the loss is enforceable.

case: Union of India v Indusind Bank Ltd
limb: s.28(a), second limb, and s.28(b) (time limits)
lawyer_note: The 1997 amendment to s.28 is not retrospective.
holding: The 1997 amendment to s.28, in force from 8 January 1997, is a substantive change that operates only prospectively, so an agreement made before that date is governed by the unamended section.

lawyer_note: The attributes of an arbitration agreement, as distinct from an expert determination.
holding: A clause sending disputes to a named person whose decision is final and binding is an arbitration agreement only if it contemplates a binding determination of the parties' substantive rights after hearing both sides; a person meant to decide as an expert, as on valuation and division of assets, is not an arbitrator.

lawyer_note: 'May be referred to arbitration' is not a binding arbitration agreement.
holding: A clause is an arbitration agreement only if it shows a present obligation to go to arbitration, so a clause referring disputes to arbitration 'if the parties so determine', or otherwise needing their further consent, is not one.

case: Vidya Drolia v Durga Trading Corporation
lawyer_note: Landlord-tenant disputes under the Transfer of Property Act are arbitrable; rent control matters are not.
holding: Landlord-tenant disputes governed by the Transfer of Property Act are arbitrable because they concern rights in personam, but those covered by rent control legislation that gives a special court or forum exclusive jurisdiction are not.

case: TRF Ltd v Energo Engineering Projects Ltd
lawyer_note: A person ineligible to be an arbitrator cannot appoint one.
holding: A person who is ineligible under s.12(5) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act to act as arbitrator, such as a party's Managing Director, cannot nominate anyone else as arbitrator.

case: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC v HSCC (India) Ltd
lawyer_note: A party with an interest in the outcome cannot unilaterally appoint a sole arbitrator.
holding: A party or official with an interest in the outcome of the dispute cannot appoint a sole arbitrator, even when it is not itself named as the arbitrator.

case: Central Organisation for Railway Electrification v ECI SPIC SMO MCML (JV)
lawyer_note: Unilateral appointment clauses violate equal treatment of parties.
holding: Equal treatment of parties applies at every stage of arbitration including appointment, so a clause letting one party unilaterally appoint a sole arbitrator raises justifiable doubts about independence and impartiality, and unilateral appointment clauses in public-private contracts violate Article 14.
